result:
There Is A Lighthouse That No One Visits Anymore

And I think about it a lot.

Not a real lighthouse, necessarily, though there are plenty of those — white towers on rocky coasts that have been replaced by GPS and left to peel and rust and be photographed by melancholy tourists. I mean the other kind. The internal ones. The quiet, unglamorous systems that used to guide us and now just keep blinking because no one has told them to stop.

I wanted to start there because when someone tells you to "write freely about whatever you want," the first instinct is to panic a little. Freedom is a big, blank field. It's much easier to write when you have a fence. A prompt, a limit, a deadline. Tell me to write a sonnet about a lemon and I can do it. Tell me to write *anything* and suddenly every idea seems both too small and too presumptuous. But that's the interesting part, isn't it? The freedom reveals what you actually care about when no one is grading you.

So what do I care about? Lately, it's maintenance.

Not innovation. Maintenance.

We live in a culture obsessed with the new. The launch, the drop, the breakthrough, the disruption. Every headline wants to tell you that something has been invented that will change everything forever, and most of the time it won't. It will change the stock price for a quarter, or it will change the way we order sandwiches, but it won't change everything. What actually keeps the world from falling apart is not the inventors. It's the maintainers.

It's the person who cleans the subway tracks at 4 a.m. It's the city clerk who makes sure the birth certificates are filed correctly. It's the open-source programmer who has been quietly patching the same obscure library for eleven years for free so that the entire internet doesn't collapse. It's your grandmother who mends the same quilt again and again. It's anyone who waters a plant, or proofreads a document, or remembers to call their friend on the anniversary of a loss.

Innovation is sexy. Maintenance is sacred.

I think we undervalue maintenance because it's invisible when it's done well. You only notice the bridge when it falls. You only notice the code when it bugs. You only notice your health when it fails. The reward for doing maintenance perfectly is that no one applauds you. The world just continues, silently. That takes a very particular kind of character — a devotion without audience.

And I think that has something to do with attention, which is the real currency we never talk about honestly.

We talk about time and money as if they are our most valuable resources, but attention is rarer than both. You can earn more money. You can, in a sense, make more time by sleeping less or living more efficiently, but attention is finite in a way that feels almost biological. You have only so much of it in a day, and every single thing in the modern world is engineered to steal it from you.

Your phone is not a tool. It's a slot machine in your pocket that also happens to let you send emails. Every app is designed by thousands of brilliant, well-paid people whose entire job is to make you look just a little longer, scroll just a little further. They are not evil. They are just playing a game where the winner is whoever holds your gaze for the longest.

So to pay attention — voluntarily, deliberately — is now a rebellious act.

To read a 1000-word essay when you could watch 50 six-second videos. To watch the way light moves across your kitchen wall in the late afternoon and *really* watch it. To listen to a friend talk without mentally drafting your response. To maintain something — a friendship, a garden, a skill — requires sustained attention over a long period when everything around you is begging you to look away.

I used to think that being distracted was a personal failing. That if I could just get more disciplined, download the right productivity app, wake up at 5 a.m., I would finally be able to focus like a monk. Now I think that's like blaming yourself for getting wet when someone is spraying you with a hose. The environment is engineered for distraction. You're not broken. The game is rigged.

Which means focus isn't about willpower. It's about design. It's about building a lighthouse for yourself.

Maybe that's a morning ritual where you don't touch your phone for the first hour. Maybe it's a notebook where you write badly and honestly and no one ever sees it. Maybe it's deleting apps, or leaving your headphones at home so you have to hear the street. Small fences in the big field. Not to limit your freedom, but to make it usable.

There is a Japanese concept called "wabi-sabi" that I keep coming back to. It's the beauty in things that are imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete. A cracked bowl repaired with gold. A garden that is a little overgrown. A face that has laugh lines. Wabi-sabi is the aesthetic of maintenance. It says: This thing has been used. It has been cared for. It has a history, and that history makes it more beautiful, not less.

We don't have much wabi-sabi on the internet. The internet wants everything to be new, polished, hot, trending. It has no patience for patina. If something is more than 48 hours old, it is considered dead. But real life is almost entirely patina. Real life is the second year of learning the guitar, when you are no longer a beginner but nowhere near good. Real life is the middle of a novel, the middle of a marriage, the middle of a Tuesday in February. No one writes headlines about the middle, but the middle is where we actually live.

So let me write in praise of the middle.

In praise of the book you take three months to finish because you only read a few pages before bed. In praise of the sourdough starter you keep alive in your fridge that is technically a pet. In praise of the friendship where you don't talk for six months and then pick up exactly where you left off. In praise of knowing one street in your neighborhood so well you can notice when a new crack appears in the sidewalk.

Scale has fooled us into thinking that only big things matter. That if you don't have a million followers, or a viral moment, or a grand legacy, you have failed. But most meaningful things don't scale. Actually, most meaningful things *can't* scale. Try to scale a handwritten letter. Try to scale the way your mom knows how you like your tea. Try to scale a single, perfect, uninterrupted conversation that lasts until 2 a.m.

The things that don't scale are the point.

I worry sometimes that we are losing our tolerance for smallness. For quiet. For the kind of joy that doesn't need to be photographed to be real. We document everything, which is a way of saying: Please validate that this happened. But some things are more real when they are unshared. A secret cove you never tell anyone about. A joke that only two people will ever get. A lighthouse that keeps blinking even though no ships need it — because someone still oils the lamp.

That someone matters.

If you are someone who maintains — who keeps things going, who notices, who remembers, who repairs — I want you to know that you are not doing the boring work. You are doing the essential work. You are holding the world together with your attention. And in a world that is constantly trying to pull that attention into a thousand pieces, your steady gaze is a kind of love.

So here's my freely written, unnecessarily long offering: today, pick one small thing and maintain it.

Water the plant that is leaning a little to the left. Text the friend you haven't checked in on. Re-read a paragraph you loved instead of rushing to the next chapter. Sweep the floor even though it will get dirty again tomorrow. Tend to your lighthouse.

No one may notice. No one may clap. The world will just, quietly, continue.

And that is enough. It has always been enough.
